blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Sharding. **Goal:** split data across machines without losing your mind, and rebalance without downtime.

rows: A horizontal slice of a dataset (a subset of rows/keys)
The physical machine/instance that holds one or more partitions
The field used to route a row to a partition
Split *rows* across stores — this is what people mean by "sharding"
Moving partitions between shards as data grows
Query hitting every shard and merging results — the anti-pattern of sharding

blocks.text: Vertical partitioning is a cheap first move: it reduces row size and lets you scale tables independently. Horizontal sharding is the real work.

sections.title: 2. How to choose a shard key

blocks.text: This is the highest-leverage decision in the entire system. Get it wrong and you'll rewrite later.
The four properties of a great shard key

items.text: **High cardinality** — many distinct values (user_id ✓, country ✗)
**Low skew / even distribution** — no hot partition (user_id ✓, "users created today" ✗)
**Co-location of related data** — everything a query needs is on one shard
**Stability** — the value doesn't change (and if it does, you know how)

blocks.text: The one-question test
**"Which single query, if it had to touch every shard, would hurt the most?"**
Then: *is that query's data co-located by my shard key?* If the answer is no, you'll have scatter-gather on your hottest path.
Shard key patterns
**A. Range / directory sharding**

items.text: Values map to ranges: `user_id < 1000` → shard 1, etc.
**Pro:** range scans and range queries stay local. Natural ordering.
**Con:** skew is easy (a hot user, a hot range); rebalancing requires moving data; range scans

blocks.text: can hit one hot shard.

items.text: Use when: data is naturally time/ID ordered and range queries dominate (logs, time-series).

blocks.text: **B. Hash / modulo sharding**

items.text: `shard = hash(key) % N`
**Pro:** near-perfect distribution, minimal metadata.
**Con:** destroys ordering (range queries fan out); reshard on N change is painful (see

blocks.text: consistent hashing).
**C. Directory / lookup-table sharding**

items.text: A mapping table: `key → shard`.
**Pro:** total control; you can move a key explicitly.
**Con:** the directory becomes a hot spot and a single point of failure; two lookups per request.

blocks.text: **D. Consistent hashing (virtually all modern systems)**

items.text: See §3. Solves the reshard problem.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Shard by a value that changes
Every change = a data migration. A user's `region` changing reshuffles everything.
Hot shards. `country` has 200 values; one country is 40% of traffic.
Shard by a field not present in the query
Uniform, but you lose locality and any ability to range-scan. (v4 UUIDs are also terrible for B-tree locality — random inserts fragment the index.) Use UUIDv7 / ULID / KSUID for time-ordered IDs.
Changing N is a migration. Use a virtual-node ring (consistent hashing).

blocks.text: The "one shard too hot" problem
A single viral user, a single huge tenant, a single hot product — one shard takes 10x the load of the others. Solutions:

items.text: **Secondary shards for hot keys** (split one key's data across many shards).
**Salt the key** (split a key's *sub*-keys, e.g. `user_id` + `bucket`).
**Read replicas** for hot-key reads (writes still serialize).
**Isolate the hot path**: move it to a dedicated store (e.g. a Redis sorted set for a trending

blocks.text: user's timeline).
The problem with `hash(key) % N`: adding a server moves ~1/N of all keys. With N=1000 and 1B keys, adding one server relocates a million keys. Unacceptable.
Consistent hashing algorithm

items.text: Hash the server IDs onto a ring (e.g. 0..2³²-1).
Hash each key onto the same ring.
A key belongs to the first server clockwise from its position.
Each server owns multiple *virtual nodes* (V-Nodes) spread around the ring (e.g. 100–200 per server).

blocks.text: **Why virtual nodes?** With only 1 point per server, the ring's key distribution is uneven (variance in gaps between servers). With 100+ points per server, distribution is near-perfect and moving one server only affects its ~1/N share.
The elegant property
Adding/removing a server only requires moving keys between that server and its neighbors on the ring — approximately 1/N of the data for N servers. Everything else stays put.

blocks.code:
NodeA(100)      NodeB(100)        NodeC(100)
   ●----●----●------●----●----●------●----●----●
   ^ keys map clockwise to the next node

   Remove NodeB → its keys move to A or C only.
   ~1/3 of data moves, not 1/3 *per-key* reshuffle of the entire dataset.

blocks.text: Rendezvous hashing (HRW — Highest Random Weight)
An alternative that's often better in practice:

items.text: For each key, compute `hash(key, server_i)` for all servers and pick the highest.
**Pros:** no ring, no virtual nodes, minimal metadata, perfect distribution, and removal is trivial.
**Cons:** O(N) computation per key (fine for hundreds of servers; use a hierarchical variant for

blocks.text: thousands).
**Practical implementations:** Cassandra's `RendezvousHash`, Dynamo, Riak, and most modern DynamoDB-style systems. Many teams implement HRW over consistent hashing.
Split brain with virtual nodes
When a server dies, its neighbor takes over its keys. If the dead server comes back, it must **not** serve stale data. Solutions:

items.text: The ring is stored in a strongly consistent store (etcd/ZooKeeper) that is updated on membership

blocks.text: change.

items.text: Nodes check membership before serving; a node removed from the ring stops accepting reads for

blocks.text: its range.

items.text: Use "gossip" protocols with incarnation numbers to detect membership changes.

blocks.text: **Shard count should be a power of 2** (so modulo and bit-masking are cheap) and **much larger than the current server count**.
Why much larger?

items.text: You want to add capacity without resharding.
Smaller shards = faster rebalancing = less downtime.
Example: 32 shards now on 8 machines (4 each). When you need 16 machines, move half the shards.
With 1000 shards on 100 machines, adding 100 machines means moving 100 shards.

blocks.text: Rule: **shards ≈ 10x your expected server count for the next 2–3 years**, but not so many that per-shard overhead (connection pools, metadata, monitoring) dominates. 1,000–10,000 shards is a typical sweet spot.
The classic approaches:
Approach 1: Make the shard count fixed and move partitions

items.text: Double the shard count: each old shard S splits into S0 and S1.
Create the new shards.
**Dual-write**: write to both old and new during the migration.
**Backfill** historical data into the new shards.
**Verify** (compare checksums/row counts).
**Cut over reads** to the new shards.
**Stop writing to old shards**; drop them.

blocks.text: Requires: idempotent writes (so dual-write retries don't duplicate), and a way to distinguish "records written during migration" from "records to backfill" (usually a high-water mark / LSN).
Approach 2: Log-structured migration
Because the data is an append-only log (Kafka, a WAL, DynamoDB Streams), you can:

items.text: Start a CDC (change data capture) stream from the old shard.
Apply it continuously to the new shard.
Take a consistent snapshot at time T.
Apply the stream from T onward.
Cut over.

blocks.text: This is how most production reshards actually work — and it's why CDC (Debezium, Kafka Connect, Fivetran) is worth learning.
Approach 3: Logical tables (DynamoDB-style)

Instead of physically moving data, change a **logical table** mapping. New writes go to the new physical tables; a background job copies history; reads hit both during the transition. The old tables are dropped after verification.
The hard part: reads during migration

items.text: **Reads must work throughout.** Usually: route reads to the *new* location if the record has been

blocks.text: migrated, else the old one. Keep a "migrated?" marker, or use the high-water mark.

items.text: **Scatter-gather during transition** is sometimes unavoidable; make it explicit and measure it.

blocks.text: A transaction spanning two shards is a distributed transaction. Options:

rows: Design so one transaction touches one shard
Coordinator asks participants to prepare, then commit
Blocks on failure, slow, coordinator is a SPOF
Heavy per-participant work, needs compensation logic
Sequence of local transactions + compensating actions
No isolation between steps, compensation is hard
Write to DB + an outbox row atomically; a relay publishes to a bus
Let each shard enforce its own uniqueness; only one wins

blocks.text: **The senior default:** design so that each transaction touches exactly one shard. Use the **outbox pattern** to reliably publish events, and **sagas** for multi-step business flows (Ch. 08).

sections.title: 7. Partitioning key pitfalls and how to avoid them

rows: One shard's CPU is 10x the others
Better key, or split hot partitions
p99 explodes as shard count grows
Co-locate by the hot query's key
Can't have a global unique constraint
ID allocation service (Snowflake IDs / per-shard prefixes), or a central registry
Use Snowflake (time + node ID) or per-shard ranges
Adding a node saturates the network
Throttle migration, use snapshots + incremental CDC

blocks.text: Snowflake-style IDs
A 64-bit ID composed of: timestamp (ms) | node ID | sequence.

items.text: Unique across nodes, roughly time-ordered (good index locality), no central coordination.
Trade-off: leaks creation time (mask the timestamp if that matters), and clock skew across nodes

blocks.text: can cause ordering surprises.
Scatter-gather and its cousin, scatter-gather-aggregate
If you must fan out, do it smartly:

items.text: **Parallel** (not serial) — issue all shard queries concurrently.
**Bounded** — cap the fan-out; if you have 1,000 shards, don't query all 1,000.
**Partial** — each shard returns its top-K; you merge and take the top-K globally.
**Cached** — cache the merged result.
**Precomputed** — better: maintain a global index (e.g., a materialized feed table).

blocks.text: If you find yourself needing frequent scatter-gather, your shard key is probably wrong, or you need a secondary/global index design (Google's "sharding at scale" approach with fan-out tables).
Secondary indexes across shards are hard: an index entry lives on a *different* shard than the row.
Approaches
**1. Local index + scatter-gather lookup** Each shard indexes its own rows; a lookup by email queries all shards and takes the first match.

items.text: Slow per lookup, but no write coordination.

blocks.text: **2. Global index table** A dedicated index store (search engine, KV store) mapping `secondary_key → shard`.

items.text: Fast lookup; but the index must be updated on every write → write amplification and a

blocks.text: consistency problem (index lags the row).
**3. Scatter-gather on write (background)** Async job updates a global index; reads may be slightly stale.

items.text: Best for read-heavy secondary access.

blocks.text: **4. Co-locate by the secondary key** If you can, choose a shard key such that the secondary access pattern is also local. Sometimes this means denormalizing the secondary key into the primary key's space.
**Important:** a global index is a *derived* structure. If it can be rebuilt, lag is tolerable. If it's authoritative, you have two systems that must agree, and you need a reconciliation process.

items.text: **Implement consistent hashing.** Write a function that maps 1M keys onto N servers with V-Nodes, and: (a) show the distribution is roughly even; (b) add a server and count how many keys moved (should be ~1/N); (c) remove a server and count moves. Compare with `hash % N` (where adding a server moves ~1 - 1/N of keys).
**Implement HRW.** Same experiment. Compare distribution quality and code complexity.

**Design a shard key.** For a messaging app (like the worked example in Ch. 20), pick the shard key and defend it against: "list all conversations for a user", "list unread counts across all conversations", "search messages by text".
**Plan a reshard.** Take your sharded schema from exercise 3 at 16 shards. Write the runbook for going to 32 shards with no downtime: which steps, in what order, how to verify, how to roll back.

blocks.text: Good: "I'd shard by tenant_id so all tenant data is co-located — that makes every tenant query local and makes per-tenant compliance and deletion easy. Trade-off: a big tenant becomes a hot shard, so I'd add a path to split a tenant onto dedicated shards. I'd use a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes and start with, say, 256 shards so I can add capacity without resharding."

Better (follow-up): "For the global search-by-name requirement, I'd add a derived global index (updated via CDC from the outbox) — it's a derived structure so brief lag is acceptable; if it must be exact, that requirement conflicts with sharding and I need to negotiate it."
Red flags: shard key with no rationale; modulo hashing with a hard-coded N and no reshard plan; assuming cross-shard transactions are fine.

selfCheck.q: **Why does `hash(key) % N` make reshardding painful, and what does consistent hashing fix?**
selfCheck.a: Adding a server changes N, which changes `key % N` for ~all keys — essentially a full data migration. Consistent hashing ensures only ~1/N of keys move.
They make the key distribution even (one point per server gives high variance in gap sizes) and make server removal move only that server's ~1/N share rather than a large arbitrary slice.

selfCheck.q: **Your shard key is `country`. What happens during a soccer final?**
selfCheck.a: The host country becomes a hot shard and gets hammered. Fix: don't shard by country (low cardinality); use a high-cardinality, low-skew key. Country should be an attribute/filters, not the partition function.

selfCheck.q: **Give one case where range sharding beats hash sharding.**
selfCheck.a: When range queries dominate (time-series logs, "everything for account X between dates"), because a range lands on one shard and stays local. Cost: skew and slower rebalancing.

The service writes the business data **and** an outbox row in a *single local transaction* (one shard, no distributed coordination). A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes to the bus, with retries and dedup. Consumers are idempotent, so at-least-once delivery is safe.

selfCheck.q: **What is scatter-gather and why does it hurt as shard count grows?**
selfCheck.a: A query that must hit every shard and merge results. Cost grows with shard count, latency becomes the slowest shard plus merge overhead, and it multiplies load across the fleet. If it's on the hot path, the shard key is wrong.

selfCheck.q: **You need a globally unique ID without a central counter. Options?**
selfCheck.a: **Snowflake-style IDs**: timestamp + node ID + sequence — time-ordered (good index locality) and collision-free across nodes with no coordination. Alternatives: UUIDv7/ULID (same idea, string form), per-shard ranges from a central allocator, or a dedicated ID service (adds a dependency).

selfCheck.q: **How would you reshard without downtime, in high-level steps?**
selfCheck.a: Double the shard count: split each old shard into two; create new shards; enable dual-write; backfill historical data (or snapshot + CDC); verify counts/checksums; cut over reads; stop old writes; delete old shards. At every step reads must be served correctly — via a "migrated?" marker or a high-water mark — and there must be a rollback plan.

selfCheck.q: **Your app needs "find user by email" and shards are by user_id. What are your options and their trade-offs?**
selfCheck.a: (a) Scatter-gather: query all shards, take the match — slow per read, no write cost. (b) Global index table (search engine or KV) mapping email → shard — fast reads, but the index is a derived structure that can lag, so writes need to update it. (c) Change the shard key to email (but that breaks the "list by user_id" hot path). (d) Denormalize email into the user row so the lookup key is local. Usually (b) or (d).

selfCheck.q: **What is a hot shard, and what are three ways to fix it?**
selfCheck.a: A shard receiving far more traffic/data than its peers. Fixes: re-shard with a better key; split the hot partition across sub-shards (salting or secondary shards); add read replicas dedicated to the hot key; or move the hot path to a purpose-built store (e.g. Redis sorted set).

selfCheck.q: **Why might you choose *not* to shard, even at high traffic?**
selfCheck.a: When the bottleneck isn't the database (it's CPU, network, or an external API); when a single Postgres on a big instance still handles the load comfortably (10–50k writes/sec is common); when the operational cost of distributed data would exceed the benefit; or when the team cannot yet operate the complexity. Sharding is expensive and hard to reverse.

selfCheck.q: **How many shards should you start with, and why?**
selfCheck.a: **~10x your expected server count** for the next few years, and a power of 2. More shards means cheaper, faster rebalancing later; fewer means each rebalance is a large, slow, risky move. Don't go so high that per-shard overhead dominates.
